extracted.intended_audience: Federal agencies, NEPA practitioners, legal counsel, and public stakeholders involved in NEPA reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble explanation and final regulatory text clarifying definitions and application guidance for NEPA implementing regulations (e.g., environmental justice, environmentally preferable alternative, extraordinary circumstances, major Federal action). Intended to guide agency application and public understanding of the revisions to 40 CFR 1508.1 and related NEPA procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "environmental justice"
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ adds a definition of 'environmental justice' to the regulations consistent with longstanding agency practice and with section 2(b) of E.O. 14096.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition clarifies and provides consistency for agencies integrating consideration of environmental justice into NEPA reviews, including analysis of potential disproportionate and adverse human health and environmental effects and ensuring meaningful engagement with affected communities. CEQ declined to define 'cumulative impacts' in the regulations (see separate entry) but will consider issuing guidance on cumulative impacts to assist agencies. CEQ also noted it may consider additional guidance to improve consistency and clarity among Federal agencies on application of the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to define "cumulative impacts"
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ declines to add a regulatory definition of 'cumulative impacts' at this time because the science is evolving and a regulatory definition would be premature and inappropriately limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ recognizes 'cumulative impacts' has meaning in environmental justice contexts (aggregate effect of multiple stressors/exposures) and will consider whether non-regulatory guidance on cumulative impacts would assist agencies conducting environmental reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmentally Preferable Alternative (§1508.1(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as 'the alternative or alternatives that will best promote the national environmental policy in section 101 of NEPA.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies identify the environmentally preferable alternative among the alternatives analyzed in an EIS (proposed action, no action, and reasonable alternatives). The definition does not require agencies to consider alternatives beyond those analyzed, does not need additional text stating the environmentally preferable alternative must be 'reasonable,' and does not require that the environmentally preferable alternative be the one that 'best strikes a balance' among competing considerations. Identifying the environmentally preferable alternative provides information to decisionmakers and the public; agencies are not required to adopt it as the final decision. The definition incorporates section 101 and is consistent with CEQ's Forty Questions guidance (1981). Commenters' suggestions to add 'reasonable' or 'economically and technically feasible' were declined because 'reasonable alternatives' are already defined and considered in the EIS process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary Circumstances (§1508.1(o))
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds a standalone definition of 'extraordinary circumstances' and examples to clarify when an action normally covered by a categorical exclusion (CE) may fall outside that category and require further analysis (EA or EIS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include substantial effects on sensitive environmental resources, disproportionate and adverse effects on communities with environmental justice concerns, effects associated with climate change, and effects on historic properties or cultural resources. CEQ uses the phrase 'substantial effects' in examples for consistency. Purpose: to screen individual actions that would normally be covered by a CE for further analysis to assess whether the action has reasonably foreseeable significant effects requiring an EIS. CEQ declined to narrow the definition, explaining agencies have long experience applying extraordinary circumstances and need flexibility to tailor extraordinary circumstances consistent with their programs. CEQ explained why it used 'substantial' rather than 'reasonably foreseeable' or 'significant' in examples to preserve efficiency in CE application and noted agencies may design extraordinary circumstances to match their needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) (§1508.1(q))
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition finalized as edited: a 'finding of no significant impact' is the agency's determination that a proposed agency action does not require the issuance of an environmental impact statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ inserted a minor editorial phrase for consistency with NEPA section 111(7) and declined to add a separate definition for a 'mitigated FONSI,' noting the meaning of a mitigated FONSI is conveyed elsewhere (§1501.6(a)). Commenters' suggestions to expand the definition to say the action will not have a significant adverse effect on any aspect of the human environment were not adopted as redundant with other provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Environment / Environment (§1508.1(r))
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ clarifies that 'human environment' and 'environment' are synonymous in the regulations and revises the definition to remove the limiting phrase 'of Americans.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition cross-references 'effects' which include ecological, aesthetic, historic, cultural, economic, social, or health effects; CEQ declined to explicitly list cultural and socio-economic conditions in this definition because of the cross-reference. CEQ explained the removal of 'of Americans' aligns the definition with the totality of NEPA section 101 and longstanding practice to evaluate effects occurring outside U.S. jurisdiction as components of the human environment, except where statutes exclude activities entirely outside U.S. jurisdiction from 'major Federal action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Lead Agency (§1508.1(s))
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines 'joint lead agency' to mean 'a Federal, State, Tribal, or local agency designated pursuant to §1501.7(c) that shares the responsibilities of the lead agency' for preparing an EA or EIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declined requests to create distinct categories for Federal vs. non-Federal joint lead agencies because the term's regulatory usage does not require such a distinction. The definition aligns with usage in NEPA section 107(a)(1)(B) and §1501.7(b)–(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead Agency (§1508.1(u))
rubrics_metrics.description: Revises 'lead agency' to 'the Federal agency that proposes the agency action or is designated pursuant to §1501.7(c) for preparing or having primary responsibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision aligns the regulatory definition with NEPA section 111(9) and expands to explicitly include EAs consistent with longstanding practice. CEQ received no adverse comments and finalized the proposed text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Federal Action (§1508.1(w)) — introductory formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Revises the introductory language to read as an 'action that the agency carrying out such action determines is' and inserts 'substantial' before 'Federal control and responsibility,' aligning with section 111(10) of NEPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ interprets 'substantial Federal control and responsibility' to mean the agency has a large amount (but not complete) control and responsibility over the action. CEQ declines to further define 'substantial' in the rule, noting case law and that determination is fact-specific; it may consider issuing future guidance to assist agencies. CEQ disagrees commenters' assertion that adding 'substantial' narrows the definition; instead it modifies the quality of control required. Agencies should continue to exercise judgment in case-by-case analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Federal Action (§1508.1(w)) — examples of activities or decisions that may qualify
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a non-exclusive list of example activities or decisions that generally include major Federal actions (reordered and revised from prior regulations). Examples include granting authorizations (permits, licenses, rights-of-way), approval or carrying out of projects, related agency decisions, management activities, and certain forms of Federal financial assistance that are more than a minimal amount and where the agency has sufficient authority or discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added an introductory clause '[e]xamples of major Federal actions generally include' to emphasize the list is illustrative and to aid agencies in fact-specific determinations. Specific editorial/clarifying changes: changed 'connected agency decisions' to 'related agency decisions'; retained both 'approval of' and 'carrying out' for projects; moved prior paragraphs to new designations. Agencies should interpret these as examples to assist case-specific judgments rather than limiting definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Federal Action (§1508.1(w)) — financial assistance example and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies that Federal financial assistance generally constitutes a major Federal action when it is more than a minimal amount and the agency has authority and discretion in a manner that could address environmental effects of the recipient's activities (e.g., ability to deny assistance or impose conditions to address environmental effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added the clause 'more than a minimal amount' to avoid conflict with statutory exclusions for minimal funding and edited wording to clarify the agency's authority to impose conditions. CEQ disagrees that this example broadens NEPA improperly: it illustrates circumstances where financial assistance meets the statutory test. Where an agency determines financial assistance is a major Federal action, it should scope NEPA review to the environmental effects it can consider given its authority. CEQ will assist agencies in evaluating such circumstances; agencies should consider statutory authorities and factual context in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Federal Action (§1508.1(w)) — exclusions from the definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopts exclusions from the definition of 'major Federal action' consistent with section 111(10)(B) of NEPA, including: (i) non-Federal actions with no or minimal Federal funding or involvement where the agency cannot control the outcome; (ii) provision of general revenue sharing funds; (iii) loans/loan guarantees/other financial assistance where the agency does not exercise sufficient control/responsibility over subsequent use or effects; and (iv) certain SBA business loan guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ replaced prior regulatory exclusions with statutory exclusions and added them in the final rule. For 'minimal Federal funding' exclusions CEQ considered but declined to adopt a numeric threshold because of programmatic variance and limited case law; agencies must evaluate 'minimal' in the specific factual context. CEQ emphasized that these exclusions do not affect situations where an agency itself is undertaking an action (e.g., issuing a permit or providing assistance) and that agencies retain responsibility to determine the proper scope of NEPA review. CEQ added cross-references and editorial clarifications to align with statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of "minimal Federal funding" and threshold comments
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ considered commenters' recommendations to establish thresholds for 'minimal Federal funding' but declined to adopt a universal numeric threshold in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the wide variety of Federal programs and limited case law defining 'minimal Federal funding,' CEQ directs agencies to continue evaluating whether funding is 'minimal' based on specific factual contexts. Some commenters supported thresholds to increase predictability; CEQ judged no single threshold appropriate across programs and retained case-specific evaluation to protect consideration of vital components of the human environment (e.g., health of children, drinking water, environmental justice concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples versus statutory text to guide application
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ provides both illustrative examples of actions that generally meet the 'major Federal action' definition and explicit statutory exclusions to guide agencies in case-by-case determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ states that combining examples and exclusions 'strikes the right balance' to assist agencies and promote consistency with section 111(10). The preamble explains why certain examples were added, clarified, or retained and why some previously used examples were moved or removed; it emphasizes that the determination is fact-specific and agencies should exercise judgment. CEQ may consider issuing further guidance where necessary (e.g., defining 'substantial').
